citation: Trinkenreich, B., Gerosa, M. A., Sarma, A., Steinmacher, I. 'Guidelines for Cultivating a Sense of Belonging to Reduce Developer Burnout'. arXiv:2605.06827v1 [cs.SE], submitted 7 May 2026. arXiv listing gives IEEE Software 42(2): 84-91 (2025), DOI 10.1109/MS.2024.3404361. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06827 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.06827). Note: PDF page footer reads 'IEEE Computer ... May/June 2022 ... © 2022 IEEE', which conflicts with the 2025 listing [uncertain].
source_tier: Peer-reviewed magazine article (IEEE Software), here seen as an arXiv preprint copy. A practitioner-oriented synthesis of the authors' own prior studies, not new data.
access_status: Fully read: PDF opened and text extracted (pdftotext); abstract page also read. Figures 1-3 are images and were not read; only their captions.
sponsor_and_incentive: Acknowledgment: 'This work is partially supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant Numbers 1900903 and 2303612.' Nothing sold. Authors are reviewing their own research programme, so some self-citation bias is plausible.
exact_quotes: 1) 'Our previous research showed that lack of belonging is associated with higher levels of burnout in software developers.' (abstract). 2) 'we conducted three studies within different software development environments, including open-source and closed-source environments' (section Deciphering Belongingness). 3) 'Based on the evidence found during quantitative analysis of belongingness in Open Source Software and IT industry contexts, we propose guidelines for leaders to cultivate belongingness in the team and thus, reduce burnout. All guidelines presented here are backed by evidence previously collected or supported by the literature.' (section Improving Belongingness). 4) 'Sense of belonging has been shown to prevent or reduce burnout by increasing job satisfaction [3].' (Resilience section). 5) 'Consistency involves regular recognition, ideally quarterly, to maintain impact without overwhelming.' (recognition). 6) 'Gartner's research [12] indicates that offering tangible benefits that cater to diverse needs, such as flexible work schedules and emotional well-being programs, enhances feelings of inclusion by as much as 38%, especially for minorities.' (benefits). 7) 'Identifying burnout signals is an open challenge for further investigation.' (monitoring section).
date_and_recency: arXiv v1 7 May 2026; IEEE Software 42(2), 2025. Underlying studies: Study 1 ICSE-SEIP 2023, Study 2 ICSE 2023, Study 3 ICSE 2024 (survey data collected before those dates; collection window not stated in this paper).
key_claims: A synthesis, no new data. Eight guidelines for leaders: (1) Timely and consistent recognition; (2) Transparent promotion rules and no glass ceiling; (3) Diverse benefits and initiatives so everyone feels included; (4) Create intentional connections through collaborative tools; (5) Conduct blameless postmortems; (6) Create optional in-person opportunities; (7) Engage newcomers through informal gatherings; (8) Monitoring and adjusting course of initiatives. Evidence basis per guideline as the paper presents it: G1 recognition rests on Study 1 via ref [3] (positive leadership feedback linked to belonging and lower burnout) and Study 3 (work appreciation correlates with belonging), plus a Gartner citation [12]; the 'ideally quarterly' cadence and the tailoring advice carry no cited data. G2 promotion rests on the Study 3 gender finding (women non-leaders report less belonging), ref [13] (earlier OSS work on becoming a maintainer) and argument; no test of a promotion intervention. G3 benefits rests on Gartner industry research [12] (38% figure), not the authors' studies. G4 connections rests on Study 2 (mutual support, knowing and being known in Linux Kernel) and a pair-rotation paper [14]. G5 blameless postmortems rests on Study 3 (psychological safety correlates with belonging) and Study 1 (generative culture) via [3]; the retrospective practice is recommended, not tested. G6 in-person rests on Study 2/3 friendship and trust characteristics plus ref [15] (psychological safety going remote); examples DevOps Days and Linux Foundation events. G7 newcomers rests on Study 2 and 3 tenure findings (longer tenure, more belonging); ice-breakers are suggested without evidence. G8 monitoring: monthly three or four question surveys are suggested; no cited evidence; burnout detection from repositories is called an open challenge [16]. Core logic: belonging correlates with job satisfaction, which correlates with lower burnout; the guidelines assume belonging can be raised by these practices and that doing so lowers burnout. The paper states no tested intervention.
headline_figures: Study 1: 3,281 survey responses, software delivery team members, proprietary software company (one global tech company), 2023 (ICSE-SEIP). Study 2: 318 survey responses, Linux Kernel contributors, ICSE 2023. Study 3: 10,781 survey responses, software development team members at another proprietary software company, ICSE 2024. Gartner: benefits 'enhances feelings of inclusion by as much as 38%' (third-party, not defined further here). 'ideally quarterly' recognition (no data). No effect sizes, correlation coefficients or p-values appear in the paper.
sample_unit_and_population: Software professionals only: team members at two proprietary-software companies (Study 1 n=3,281; Study 3 n=10,781; roles include leaders and non-leaders) and Linux Kernel contributors (Study 2 n=318, mix of volunteers and paid). Individual survey respondents, cross-sectional.
observed_vs_stated: All self-reported survey responses (belonging, satisfaction, burnout, psychological safety). Associations are statistical correlations from models, not observed behaviour or experiments. Guidelines themselves are recommendations.
what_it_measures_or_defines: Burnout: 'feelings of exhaustion on physical, emotional, and cognitive fronts' (paraphrase of the paper's text). Belongingness: how far people feel part of a group or fit it (Hagerty and Patusky): feeling valued and accepted, and fitting in. Study 1 measured burnout by survey, instrument not named in this paper [uncertain]. Study 3 used SOBI (Sense of Belonging instrument); Study 2 used Sense of Virtual Community.
mechanism_or_cause: Lack of belonging leads to isolation and lower job satisfaction, which is associated with higher burnout. Study 1 key finding: organizational culture, climate for learning, belonging and inclusiveness are positively associated with work satisfaction, 'which in turn is associated with Reduced Burnout'. Belonging is also said to support resilience. Burnout is treated as an outcome of low satisfaction and isolation, not of workload, which is not discussed.
interventions_and_effects: None tested. The eight guidelines are recommendations derived from correlational findings and literature. No effect sizes for any intervention. Only numeric effect claim is Gartner's 'as much as 38%' for inclusion from tangible benefits (not belonging or burnout). Factors found associated with belonging: Study 2: intrinsic motivations (kinship, fun) positive, English proficiency positive, tenure positive, power distance negative, gender minorities weaker. Study 3: psychological safety and work appreciation positive, tenure positive, power distance negative, women lower (women non-leaders lower than women leaders).
transfer_to_software_teams: Evidence is from software engineers (two companies, plus Linux Kernel), so transfers directly in population, but two single-company case studies and one OSS project limit generalisation. Gartner, pair rotation, and psychological-safety-remote references are from other or mixed contexts. The belonging-to-burnout link comes from one company (Study 1).
limitations_stated: The paper does not have a limitations section. Related statements: 'While numerous variables can influence these initiatives' outcomes, evaluating their effectiveness consistently remains essential.' On burnout detection from repositories: 'the effectiveness of these techniques is not universal due to contextual factors not possible to collect via archival data.' 'Identifying burnout signals is an open challenge for further investigation.'
counter_evidence: Not discussed in the paper. Observations: correlational cross-sectional surveys cannot show that belonging causes less burnout (reverse causation or common-cause plausible); satisfaction is the stated mediator; workload and job demands, the main drivers in other burnout models, are absent; guidelines untested; the same group authored all underlying studies. Stronger burnout-intervention evidence (e.g. organisation-directed interventions) should be taken from other sources.
verification_status: Eight guideline headings and the study sample sizes: checked in the opened PDF. Study findings quoted: checked as summarised in this paper only; the original ICSE papers [3],[8],[9] were NOT opened [uncertain]. Gartner 38%: not checked against Gartner [uncertain]. Journal reference and year: from arXiv listing; PDF footer says 2022 [uncertain]. Burnout instrument used in Study 1: not stated [uncertain].
usable_claim: Trinkenreich and colleagues, drawing on their own surveys of 3,281 and 10,781 developers at two companies and 318 Linux Kernel contributors, report that sense of belonging is associated with higher job satisfaction and lower burnout, and propose eight practices for leaders. These are recommendations from correlational data and have not been tested as interventions.
do_not_use: Do not say the guidelines are proven to reduce burnout or cite effect sizes. Do not use the Gartner 38% figure as evidence about burnout or belonging. Do not use 'ideally quarterly' recognition as an evidence-based cadence. Do not present it as new research.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the essays' text in this task [uncertain]. The paper is about belonging and human-team practices, not agents, so overlap with 'Overseeing Agents Is the Tiring Part', the trust essay or 'Checking Isn't Catching' is likely low.
